resources.string: Explore how load impedance affects reflection and SWR, and how impedance changes along a transmission line.
Green marker (Γ(d)) — reflection coefficient at the selected point on the line.
Solid arrows show the reflection vectors. The dashed circle of radius |Γ| shows constant SWR.
Drag the yellow marker to change the load. Drag the green marker or move the distance slider to explore the line.
d = %1$s λ · Γ at this point = %2$s · lossless line
Chart anatomy — how to read the lines and circles
Smith chart showing the resistive axis, constant resistance circles and reactance arcs.
The horizontal axis is purely resistive. At the center, Z = Z₀ and Γ = 0. The left edge is a short circuit and the right edge is an open circuit.
Each resistance circle holds the normalized resistance r constant. The upper half is inductive and the lower half is capacitive.
Each reactance arc holds the normalized reactance x constant. A series inductor or capacitor moves the point along a circle of constant r.

Smith chart grid highlighting the reference impedance Z₀, a constant-resistance circle, and a constant-reactance arc. On the right, the up arrow indicates inductive reactance (+j) and the down arrow indicates capacitive reactance (−j).
The outer boundary represents total reflection, where |Γ| = 1. Reflection magnitude and SWR are constant along the dashed circle.
Constant-resistance circles (r = const). Along each circle, reactance x changes while resistance r stays fixed.
Constant-reactance arcs (x = const). Along each arc, resistance r changes while reactance x stays fixed. Reactance is inductive (+j) above the axis and capacitive (−j) below it.
The reference impedance Z₀ sets the scale of the grid. At the center, Z = Z₀, so Γ = 0 and there is no reflection.
Cable values are typical. Check the datasheet for the exact cable or measure its velocity factor.
